doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Developing the left hand and how songs got written
summary: He worked on technique alone and had no deadlines; Audre says he taped songs for the label.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I remember when you started really concentrating on developing your left hand as well as your right hand. That was a kind of major change.
In the ‘50s, this was, or later?
were you studying with a teacher, or just your own...
Always by yourself. You’re always doing this stuff by yourself.
Did the first success, the first public acceptance of you as a bandleader, spur you to write more? Did that...
No. I wasn’t aware of that. I was never expected to write more. I don’t think...

So when you had new record dates coming up... Well, I guess you did quite a few in 1958 and 1959 to fulfill your obligations to Prestige. But when you had deadlines, did you operate well on a deadline, writing new stuff...

What he did... You usually wrote a bunch of things, recorded them on a little cassette, and then gave the record company a call and said, “I have these.” Isn’t that how it was done? That’s how I remember it.
Well, that’s how it was done.
